title: The real presence (CCC 1373–1381)
hook: Christ present in the word, the priest, the people, and above all under the species

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacrifice and memorial, and the word anamnesis. Your line was present, not repeated.

A man in a work jacket comes in out of the rain, dips his fingers in the holy water, walks halfway down the aisle, and stops. His right knee goes down to the floor for a second, his eyes on a small gold box at the front with a lamp burning beside it. He didn't kneel to the altar, or the crowd, or the building. He knelt toward that box, because of what the Church teaches is kept inside it. Today's word is the reason for that knee.
screen: `IN FROM THE RAIN.` → `ONE KNEE TO THE FLOOR.` → `TOWARD A SMALL GOLD BOX.`

segments.voice: Day ninety-nine taught the knee itself; now, the why. Christ is present to his Church in many ways, the Catechism says. In his word. In the Church's prayer, because he said, in the Douay-Rheims, "where there are two or three gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In the poor, the sick, the imprisoned. In the sacraments. In the sacrifice of the Mass, and in the person of the priest. But above all, he is present under the Eucharistic species, the bread and wine, and that presence the Catechism calls unique. Quoting the Council of Trent, it says the body and blood of Christ, with his soul and divinity, the whole Christ, are contained in the sacrament truly, really, and substantially. Three words, each shutting a door. Truly: not as a picture. Really: not only in the mind of the believer. Substantially: in what the bread and wine are, not just how they look. The Church calls this change transubstantiation. The presence begins at the consecration and lasts as long as the species do, and Christ is whole and entire in each of them and in every part. Behind it all is Jesus's line in John's Gospel: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." So the Church shows adoration by genuflecting or bowing deeply, and keeps the Eucharist in the tabernacle, for the sick and for prayer. Quoting Thomas Aquinas, the Catechism says this presence can't be grasped by the senses, only by faith. That's the knee in the aisle.
screen: `MANY WAYS PRESENT.` · `ABOVE ALL, UNDER BREAD AND WINE.` · `TRULY, REALLY, SUBSTANTIALLY.` · `KNEELING, AND KEPT FOR PRAYER.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: If you're near a church, find the tabernacle with its lamp and bend one knee slowly, as if for the first time; if not, do it where you are, or simply bow your head, the deep bow the Catechism names too. Then sit and say the three words, one per breath: truly, really, substantially. If you pray, stay in adoration a while; if you don't, just notice what it's like to kneel to something.
Real presence. Christ present in many ways, and above all under the bread and wine: truly, really, substantially. Today's word.
Your line: truly, really, substantially. Seven days, from many rites to the real presence. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Latin-rite churches people customarily genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering or leaving a pew, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, with the host displayed in a monstrance for silent prayer.

chat.says: Why did that man kneel toward the little gold box in your church?
options: The tabernacle; Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the Eucharist kept there.
It's where the church keeps its most valuable relics and the parish records.
He was bowing to the priest's chair, as a sign of respect for the pastor.
chat.meaning: The Catechism teaches Christ is present truly, really and substantially under the bread and wine, so the Church kneels and keeps the Eucharist in the tabernacle.

transubstantiation.meaning: the Church's word for the change in what bread and wine are

species.meaning: the bread and wine as they appear

Council of Trent.meaning: a Church council the Catechism quotes on this presence

consecration.meaning: the moment at Mass when this presence begins

genuflecting.meaning: bending one knee to the floor
